ca_capstone_area.blurb: A small pocket of boulders inside Culp Valley, a desert bouldering zone in San Diego County at roughly 3,700 feet. Ten problems are spread across a cone-shaped hill and the ground beside it, close to the highway, so there is very little walking once the car is parked. The grades run wide for such a small cluster: a couple of easy V1s, a middle band from V2 to V5, and a handful of hard problems up to V8. The best-known line is a steep V5+ near the top of the hill. Expect short, athletic problems rather than tall ones, and bring a pad.

ca_highball_boulder.blurb: One of the more prominent boulders in the Snow Valley West bouldering zone, up in the San Bernardino Mountains near Big Bear at about 6,100 feet. Its ten problems are gentle: mostly VB through V1 with a couple of V3s, which makes it a friendly warm-up block rather than a project wall. Despite the name, the rock is not especially tall, though it is among the taller stones in the neighbourhood, and a bolt on top lets you top-rope anything that feels too high. Landings are described as good, so a pad or two is plenty. The boulder is a short walk uphill from the pull-out and suits beginners.

ca_phobos_deimos_cliff.blurb: A compact, steep crack wall in Tuolumne Meadows, Yosemite, standing at roughly 8,700 feet near Tenaya Lake. Ten routes are split between traditional lines and a few bolted ones, with a couple around 5.9, a solid block in the 5.11 range, three at 5.12 and one harder outlier. The two namesake three-pitch crack climbs are the draw, with hands, fists and offwidth on firm, clean rock. The cliff faces south, so it warms up well, though it picks up shade later in the day. The approach is a talus-and-forest grunt along a marked trail, and afternoon thunderstorms can build fast at this elevation.

ca_lidija_pollen_grain_boulder.blurb: A big granite block in the Pollen Grains sector of the Buttermilks, on the quieter north side of the main Bishop-area bouldering zone at about 6,400 feet. Ten problems cover a wide spread, from an easy V0 through the middle grades to a few at V5 to V7 and one standout near V10. Many of the lines are tall, reaching 20 feet or more, with blocky landings, so bring several pads and capable spotters. The movement mixes slab technique with steeper power sequences. It sees fewer people than the Buttermilks main area, and fall through spring is the usual window for good friction.

ca_larry_flynt_memorial_boulder.blurb: The larger of two named boulders in a small cluster in the Queen Mountain part of Joshua Tree National Park, at roughly 4,800 feet. Most of the ten routes here are short boulder problems, from VB up to about V4, plus three easy trad lines in the 5.5 to 5.7 range. It is a remote spot: reaching it means a long contour walk beyond another boulder group and then a climb of about 150 yards up the side of a pale drainage, so expect a quiet day with few other climbers. Bring pads, water and a sense of direction, and treat it as a destination in itself rather than a stop-off.

ca_hidden_eagle.blurb: A small multipitch wall in the southern Sierra foothills, above Chilkoot Lake near Shuteye Peak and Bass Lake. The ten routes are mostly traditional lines of two to three pitches, with a few bolted ones, and the grades stay in a friendly range from easy fifth class up to 5.10. Expect cracks, knobby faces and slabs, with supplemental bolts and bolted belays between pitches. The walk in follows the lake shore and then a cairned trail up a drainage, finishing with some brush near the base. Summer days can be hot and the wall gets a lot of sun, so carry plenty of water. Descent is on foot over the top.

ca_bar_rock.blurb: The tallest block at the Bar, a river-side bouldering zone in the Auburn State Recreation Area, across the water from the Quarry. Ten climbs share the rock: seven boulder problems, mostly V3 to V7, and three bolted sport lines. The rock stands above the smaller boulders around it, so some of the problems are on the high side and a good set of pads is worthwhile. It sits low, at around 600 feet, beside the river. Most of the bouldering around here falls in the moderate-to-hard range, which makes Bar Rock better suited to experienced boulderers than to beginners.

ca_lower_falls_2.blurb: A south-facing cirque of volcanic basalt below the main drop at Fossil Falls, off the highway in the Coso Range of Inyo County at about 3,200 feet. Almost all of the ten routes are traditional, with one top-rope line, and they run from an easy 5.5 up through 5.9 and 5.10 to a few at 5.11, on walls up to about 80 to 100 feet. The basalt has been polished smooth by ancient water, with cracks, roofs and bulges, and a brittle horizontal band near the ground that needs careful gear placement. It is less visited than the upper cliffs. Sun is strong in summer, so choose cooler months.
